finalRewrite.answer: Clawback (CAP-0035, Protocol 17) lets an issuer burn a specified amount of its asset from a holder's clawback-enabled trustline, or an entire clawback-enabled claimable balance, without the holder's cooperation; the amount is burned, not returned. The issuer must set AUTH_REVOCABLE, then AUTH_CLAWBACK_ENABLED, before trustlines are created. It is an intentional, issuer-only regulatory tool, not a vulnerability, so holders carry issuer counterparty risk; XLM and unflagged assets are unaffected.
keyFacts: An issuer can burn a set amount from a clawback-enabled trustline without holder consent.
CAP-0035 introduced clawback in Protocol 17.

It is intentional and issuer-only, so holders bear issuer risk; it is not a vulnerability.
avoid: Do NOT attribute clawback to another protocol or CAP, or to Soroban.
Do NOT claim clawed-back assets return to the issuer, that any account can claw back, or that XLM is clawbackable.

finalRewrite.answer: SEP-8 lets an issuer require approval of each transaction for a classic regulated asset. The issuer sets Authorization Required and Revocable (clawback is optional) and publishes regulated, approval_server and approval_criteria in stellar.toml. The wallet posts its signed transaction to the approval server, which returns success, revised, pending, action_required or rejected. The wallet re-signs revisions and submits; the server does not. No Soroban is needed.
keyFacts: SEP-8 lets an issuer require approval-server sign-off on each regulated-asset transaction.
The issuer sets Authorization Required and Revocable (clawback optional) and declares regulated and approval_server in stellar.toml.
The wallet posts its signed transaction, and inspects and re-signs any revised one.
The wallet, not the approval server, submits the final transaction; Soroban is not needed.
avoid: Do NOT call SEP-8 a KYC or authentication standard.
Do NOT substitute AUTH_CLAWBACK_ENABLED for the required AUTH_REVOCABLE.
Do NOT say the approval server submits the transaction.

finalRewrite.answer: MPP is an HTTP-402 payment protocol. On Stellar, Charge settles a SAC transfer per request on-chain, and Session uses a funded channel with cumulative off-chain commitments. An API advertises payment through an OpenAPI 3.1 document with x-payment-info.offers, but the runtime 402 challenge is authoritative for price, token, network and expiry. MPP and x402 both use HTTP 402 with different payloads and headers; never relabel one as the other.
